title: AI’s Global Buildout Is Redrawing Trade Flows
summary: LPL Research explores the impact that the AI buildout has on international trade and economic growth.
body_markdown:
# The AI Buildout Is Reshaping Global Trade


[Dr. Jeffrey Roach](https://www.lpl.com/research/research-team/jeffrey-j-roach.html) | Chief Economist


Last Updated: November 05, 2026


The artificial intelligence (AI) investment boom is beginning to leave a clear imprint on U.S. trade, computer inflation, and the labor market as highlighted in our recent[Econ Market Minute](https://www.lpl.com/research/econ-market-minute/ai-the-fed-and-france-three-shifts-to-watch.html) .


The trade deficit subtracted 3.3 percentage points from Q3 economic growth. Excluding “Liberation Day” distortions, last quarter’s negative impact was the largest since 1947!


In this piece, I explain why the trade deficit has widened so dramatically. American technology companies are pouring capital into data centers and computing capacity, but much of the physical equipment needed to build that infrastructure is produced abroad. Servers, semiconductors, storage systems, networking equipment, and other advanced electronics are increasingly flowing into the U.S., creating an unusual dynamic: an investment boom largely driven by American companies is becoming an important source of demand for manufacturers outside the U.S.


AI has become one of international trade’s principal drivers. And this happened despite formidable trade barriers. The average U.S. tariff rate rose from 2.9% in January 2025 to 14.8% by December. Dallas Federal Reserve (Fed) researchers estimate that, all else equal, the increase in tariffs would have reduced U.S. imports by approximately 12%. Some of the resilience reflected companies rushing imports ahead of tariffs, but booming AI investment was another important counterweight. Demand for computing equipment has simply been strong enough to overcome some of the drag from substantially higher trade barriers.


### The AI Buildout is Drastically Reshaping International Trade


*Source: LPL Research, Census Bureau 11/04/26*
*Disclosures: Past performance is no guarantee of future results.*


The AI boom is also changing where America buys its goods. China's share of U.S. imports fell from 13.4% in 2024 to 9% in 2025, while countries including Taiwan, Mexico, Vietnam, and India gained ground. Growth in technology imports from Taiwan and Mexico has substantially exceeded the decline from China, suggesting the pattern reflects more than a simple reshuffling of existing trade. It represents new demand alongside the reorientation of global supply chains.


Taiwan occupies a particularly important position because of its role in advanced semiconductors and computing. Mexico's growing role tells a different, but complementary, story. Much of the computing equipment used in U.S. data-center construction has been imported through Mexico, according to the Dallas Fed, reinforcing the country's position inside North America's technology manufacturing hub.


There is even evidence that AI demand is spilling into prices. Heavy demand for memory chips used in data centers has helped push consumer-electronics prices higher, reversing their decades-long tendency to decline. That underscores the scale of the investment cycle: AI infrastructure is competing for some of the same technology components used elsewhere in the economy.


## The International Investment Angle


For investors, these changing trade patterns broaden the AI story beyond the familiar group of U.S. technology companies. American hyperscalers may be writing many of the checks for new data centers, but an expanding portion of the manufacturers are overseas.


That creates an important argument for international diversification that goes beyond cheaper valuations. Taiwan offers exposure to semiconductors and advanced-computing supply chains. Mexico is becoming more deeply integrated into North American technology manufacturing. Vietnam, India, and other Asian economies are gaining share as global supply chains continue to diversify away from China.


There is an interesting macroeconomic twist. Imports subtract from U.S. gross domestic product (GDP) accounting, so the AI infrastructure boom can widen the trade deficit and weigh down U.S. growth even while signaling strong underlying business investment. At the same time, American investment can support production, capital spending and incomes in countries supplying the equipment.


For investors heavily concentrated in U.S. equities, that is worth considering. AI may be led, and financed by America, but the economic benefits are increasingly global. The next stage of the AI investment cycle may create opportunities not only among the companies designing models and operating data centers, but also among the international companies and economies supplying the semiconductors and electronics needed.
